messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Ellis was 67, a school principal in a midsized American suburb, a husband of forty years, and by his own account a man who had once prided himself on being steady under pressure. That certainty was shaken on a winter evening when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan, spinning him into the median hard enough to make the airbags explode across his face and chest. In the seconds after impact he heard metal shrieking, shouted fragments from people outside, and the sudden slam of other cars braking nearby. The collision was life-threatening enough that, in the days afterward, the ordinary sight of cars hit by accident on the roadside, a burst of shouting, or any loud noise would seize him by the chest before he could reason with himself. Those moments did not just startle him; they pulled him straight back into the crash, and he would feel the terrifying scene coming over him again in flashes he could not shut off.

What Martin found most unsettling was that the memory would not stay in words. He could describe that he had been hit, but the frightening event never settled into a tidy story he could tell his wife or the therapist he finally saw. Instead it returned like a film, over and over, with the crushed hood, the violent jolt, and the helplessness of knowing he could not stop what was happening. At times, when he tried to think about it, he felt as if it were happening right now, not years ago, and that reliving left him with the conviction that he had been permanently changed for the worse. He also compared himself bitterly to other people he knew, certain somebody else would not have gotten into such a situation, and that thought deepened his sense that he had become a lesser version of himself.

From there, his days narrowed. Martin came to believe the world was a dangerous place and that danger could appear without warning, so he began watching for signs of it everywhere. If a hallway announcement at school lasted longer than expected, if a student was late to an appointment, or if a phone call dragged on without an answer, he assumed something bad was happening. The same dread spread into nights at home, where he could not relax even in his own living room, and sleep became broken and shallow. When he felt the alarm rising, he forced himself to think only positive thoughts, ate excessively to take the edge off, and told himself these were small disciplines that should help. In practice, they only gave him a brief sense of control; by pushing away the fear and filling himself with food, he became even more on guard for the next hint of trouble.

That vigilance did not calm him. Martin found himself scanning for shouting in the school building, flinching at loud noises from dropped books or slamming doors, and dreading any scene that reminded him of a crash. If he heard raised voices from the front office or saw a wreck on the morning commute, the old images came back with more force, and the return of those images confirmed his belief that the world was dangerous and that he was damaged. The more that happened, the more he avoided going to work unless absolutely necessary, rearranging meetings and stepping away from the building whenever he could. He was embarrassed by how often he checked the parking lot before crossing it and how tense he felt moving through normal routines, but he also felt he had no better option.

Over the following months, the cycle hardened. Each time Martin stayed home, skipped an unnecessary commitment, or swallowed his fear with another round of positive self-talk and food, he told himself he was managing. Yet the relief was short-lived, and the avoidance left him more isolated from the school he had led for years. It also fed the very beliefs that haunted him: if he could not cope with an ordinary workday, perhaps he really had been permanently altered; if a delayed text or a loud hallway noise could set off panic, perhaps he was right that danger was everywhere. His memories kept returning in vivid, wordless bursts, his body stayed keyed for the next threat, and the more he lived around those reactions, the more brittle his world became.

By the time Martin sought help, his wife had become concerned that he was disappearing into himself—sleeping poorly, eating too much in the evenings, and avoiding the school whenever possible. He came in because he was tired of living as though every delay were an omen and every sudden noise a warning, and because he feared he was losing the life he had built. What he hoped for, and what frightened him most, was the possibility that he might never again feel safe enough to stand in a classroom, hear a shout, or drive through an intersection without the crash rushing back.
